explanation: Shopify pauses payouts when it needs to verify your account, bank details, or review recent chargebacks. Your customers can still check out — you just cannot receive the transfer yet.
steps: Read the yellow or red banner at the top of Shopify admin — it usually names the exact reason.
Check the store owner's email (and spam) for a request from Shopify Payments.
Go to Settings → Payments → Shopify Payments → View payouts and confirm the hold reason.
Open Settings → Payments and confirm the bank account name, transit, and account numbers match your bank exactly.
If chargebacks made your balance negative, resolve open disputes first. Payouts resume once the balance is no longer negative.

match_phrases: this store is currently unable to accept payments
explanation: Checkout has no active primary payment provider. Extra methods like PayPal Express do not replace a card gateway — customers will see that the store cannot accept payments.
steps: Go to Settings → Payments.
If Shopify Payments is available in your country, click Complete account setup and finish identity verification.
If Shopify Payments is not available, click Choose third-party provider and add Stripe, PayPal Payments Complete, or another primary gateway.
Confirm the provider status reads Active — not Draft, Test, or Incomplete.
Place a test order (or use Bogus Gateway on a development store) to confirm the Pay now button works.

explanation: Test mode (or Bogus Gateway) accepts fake cards only. Live customers will be declined until you switch the provider to production credentials.
steps: Go to Settings → Payments.
Open your credit-card provider and check for a Test mode toggle.
Turn Test mode off. Save.
If you use a third-party gateway, replace test API keys with live keys from that provider's dashboard.
Run a small real transaction and refund it to confirm live charges work.

explanation: Shopify could not match the payout account to the legal business name on file. A single character mismatch (Inc. vs Ltd., nickname vs legal name) is enough to reject the account.
steps: Open Settings → Payments → Shopify Payments → Manage.
Click Edit next to the payout bank account.
Copy the account holder name, transit/routing, and account number from a bank statement — do not type from memory.
The name must match the legal business name on your Shopify Payments account, not a DBA or personal nickname.
Save and wait for micro-deposit or instant verification. Payouts stay held until the bank verifies.

explanation: A customer asked their bank to reverse a charge. Shopify holds that amount (plus a fee) and can pause payouts if the balance goes negative.
steps: Go to Orders and filter by Chargebacks, or open Settings → Payments → View payouts → Disputes.
Open the dispute before the respond-by date shown — missing it means an automatic loss.
Upload proof: fulfillment receipt, tracking that shows delivered, order confirmation, and any customer messages.
Submit the response and monitor the status. Wins usually post in 60–75 days.
If the balance is negative, add a reserve or wait for new sales — payouts resume when the balance is positive.

explanation: Shopify Payments cannot finish setup (or has paused payouts) until the store owner proves who they are and that the business is real.
steps: Sign in as the store owner — staff accounts usually cannot submit KYC documents.
Click the banner on the admin home, or go to Settings → Payments → Complete account setup.
Upload a government ID plus a matching bank statement or void cheque.
If you sell as a company, also upload articles of incorporation that match the legal name on the account.
Wait for the review (often 1–3 business days). Watch the store-owner email for follow-up questions.

explanation: The card was authorized but not captured. If your store uses manual capture, you must take the payment before the authorization expires (usually 7 days).
steps: Open the order. If it says Authorized or Payment pending, the money is not in your account yet.
Click Capture payment and confirm the amount.
To stop doing this by hand: Settings → Payments → Manage → Payment capture → Automatically capture payment for orders.
If the authorization expired, ask the customer to place the order again or send an invoice.
Check that no fraud app is holding capture on high-risk orders.

explanation: PayPal is disconnected, restricted, or still in an incomplete onboarding state. It will not appear at checkout until the account is active and the emails match.
steps: Go to Settings → Payments and find PayPal.
If it says Reconnect or Incomplete, click it and sign in with the business PayPal email (personal accounts are often rejected).
In PayPal, confirm the account can receive payments and is not limited.
Turn PayPal off, save, then turn it back on if the button still does not appear.
Test checkout in an incognito window. Shop Pay and Apple Pay are separate — they will not fix a PayPal outage.

match_phrases: unable to process in this currency
explanation: The store currency and the payment provider's supported currencies do not line up, or a Market is presenting a currency the gateway cannot charge.
steps: Note the store currency under Settings → General → Store defaults.
Open Settings → Payments and confirm the provider supports that currency.
If you sell in multiple currencies, enable Shopify Payments multi-currency or Markets, and check each market's payment methods.
Do not change the store currency on a live store without a migration plan — existing product prices and reports will break.
Place a test order from the affected country using a VPN or Markets preview.

synonyms: bank asked for a code and it failed
explanation: The customer's bank required 3-D Secure (common in Europe). The charge was not declined for funds — authentication never finished.
steps: Open the order or abandoned checkout. Look for Authentication failed or 3D Secure in the timeline.
Ask the customer to retry and complete the bank prompt (app approval or SMS code).
Confirm Shopify Payments or your gateway has 3DS enabled — do not turn it off in regions that require SCA.
If only one bank fails repeatedly, have the customer try another card or Shop Pay.
Check that checkout apps are not breaking the 3DS redirect popup.

explanation: Declines can be the customer's bank, your fraud filters, or a gateway still in a review state. A sudden spike usually means settings or a provider hold — not random bad cards.
steps: Open Analytics → Reports → Payments or the Payments dashboard and note the decline reason codes.
Go to Settings → Payments → Manage and confirm you are not in test mode and the account is not under review.
Review Settings → Payments → Fraud protect (and any third-party fraud app). Loosen rules that auto-cancel medium-risk orders.
Enable a backup method (PayPal or Shop Pay) so a card decline is not a lost sale.
If almost every card fails, contact the provider from Settings → Payments → More actions → Contact provider.

explanation: Shop Pay only appears when Shopify Payments is the primary gateway and Shop Pay is toggled on. Third-party-only stores cannot offer it.
steps: Confirm Shopify Payments is your primary provider under Settings → Payments.
On that same page, turn on Shop Pay.
Shop Pay is unavailable in some countries and on password-protected stores that block Shop domain checks.
If installments are missing, open Shop Pay → Manage and complete Shop Pay Installments onboarding.
Test in an incognito window on mobile — Shop Pay is most visible there.

explanation: The third-party gateway rejected Shopify's request because the API keys are wrong, restricted, or were rotated on the provider side.
steps: Log into the provider dashboard (Stripe, Authorize.net, etc.) and confirm the account is active.
Create a fresh set of live secret and publishable keys.
In Shopify go to Settings → Payments → Manage, remove the old keys, paste the new ones, and save.
Turn off any test/sandbox toggle on both sides.
Run a $1 real charge and refund it. If it still fails, use More actions → Contact provider from that page.

match_phrases: this payment method is not available for your location
explanation: The Market or payment provider does not offer that method in the customer's country. The cart is fine — the payment method list is empty for that location.
steps: Identify the customer's country from the abandoned checkout.
Go to Settings → Markets and open that market. Confirm it is published and has payment methods assigned.
In Settings → Payments, check which methods are restricted by country.
Add a method that works there (local cards, PayPal, or a local provider).
Preview checkout with that country selected in the order address.

explanation: Express wallets need Shopify Payments (or a compatible gateway), HTTPS on the custom domain, and the button enabled on product and cart pages.
steps: Settings → Payments → Shopify Payments → turn on Apple Pay and Google Pay.
Online Store → Themes → Customize → Theme settings → Cart / Checkout and enable dynamic checkout buttons.
Online Store → Domains: the primary domain must show as Connected and issued a valid SSL certificate.
Apple Pay only appears in Safari (or Chrome with a saved card on supported OS versions).
If it vanished after a theme edit, restore the buy-buttons section — custom product pages often drop the wallet button.

explanation: Shopify (or the gateway) is holding a percentage of each payout as a risk reserve. New stores and stores with high refund or chargeback rates see this most often.
steps: Open Settings → Payments → View payouts and click a payout. Look for a Reserve line item.
Read the email that announced the reserve — it includes the percentage and how long it lasts.
Keep chargebacks and refunds low, fulfill on time, and answer Shopify's information requests.
Do not open a second Shopify Payments account to dodge a reserve — that can suspend both.
If the reserve looks wrong, contact Shopify Payments support from the payouts page with the payout ID.

match_phrases: payment failed for your shopify invoice
synonyms: shopify charged my card and failed
explanation: This is Shopify charging you for the plan or apps — not customer checkout. A failed Shopify invoice can freeze the admin and take the storefront offline.
steps: Go to Settings → Billing (the store owner may be the only one who can see it).
Update the card on file and pay the outstanding invoice.
If the store is frozen, paying the invoice usually unfreezes it within a few minutes.
Check for a failed app charge that is separate from the monthly plan.
After it is current, place a test order to confirm checkout was not affected.

explanation: Manual methods create unpaid orders that you mark as paid later. They never charge a card automatically and will not replace a real gateway.
steps: Settings → Payments → Manual payment methods → Add manual payment method.
Choose Cash on Delivery, Bank deposit, or Custom, and write clear instructions the customer will see.
Save. Manual methods appear below card options at checkout.
When the money actually arrives, open the order and click Mark as paid.
Do not rely on COD alone if you also need Shopify Payments features like Shop Pay.
